newsitem.title: UK: Europe, U.S. bonds set to pull apart.
newsitem.headline: Europe, U.S. bonds set to pull apart.

text.p: European bond markets have been tied to the U.S. interest rate cycle in recent months, but there is room for some breakout in the months to come, economists said on Friday.
"We see the European markets underperforming against the U.S., and the U.S./German spread narrowing significantly," said Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
The differing fates of European and U.S. markets will develop against a backdrop of falling global bond prices, economists said.

"Our valuation models show Treasuries at the longer end of the curve are reasonably close to fair value," said Bevan. "The starting position for the European core markets is significantly overvalued," he added.
Bevan said the 10-year T-note/Bund spread would narrow from its current 115 basis point level to 100 basis points on a three-month horizon, and 70 basis points over six months.
But Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe in London, said, in contrast, that Europe would outperform the U.S. over the next three months.
"The Treasury market is looking hard for signs of an economic slowdown in the U.S., but it is not going to be sufficient for it to outperform Germany," he said.
Fishwick saw the U.S./German spread widening to 125-130 basis points by July.
The main focal points for the markets remain U.S. interest rates, U.S. economic indicators, and the progress of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), economists said.

The Fed will attempt to keep a bounding U.S. economy in check by raising interest rates at the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on May 20, and this is already reflected in the market, economists said.
Next week's batch of data will do nothing to dissuade the market from that view, they added.
Markets are awaiting the release of the first quarter U.S. employment cost index on Tuesday, and a cluster of other key indicators will culminate in April employment numbers on Friday.
"The figures will paint a fairly strong picture of an economy that is quite robust," said Gwyn Hacche, senior European economist at HSBC James Capel in London.
There will be little to support Treasuries, economists said, and the only question is whether or not Germany and core Europe will fall faster or slower than U.S. bonds on the way down.
Those in the U.S. camp have gained further impetus in the shorter term from the latest twists in the EMU debate, economists said.

European bond markets opened softer on Friday after the release on Thursday of a poll showing the French centre-right government with only a slim majority ahead of a snap election called this week for May 25 and June 1.
The centre-right government is regarded as more EMU-friendly than the opposition Socialists.
"The centrists have not done as well as everyone hoped (in the poll)," said Fishwick. "This will affect holders of long-dated Bunds and the German curve will steepen."

Economists also remain cynical about the release on Wednesday of the European Commission's deficit to GDP forecasts, which showed only Italy and Greece were currently missing deficit to GDP targets this year to qualify for EMU.
Fishwick said the "obviously cosmetic report" was a further indication that "monetary union is going to be soft when it happens".
But Hacche at James Capel remains neutral on the U.S./Germany spread until the summer.
"Over the next few months we see little change in the spread. But in the second half of the year it will narrow, as the U.S. economy slows down."
